Adult Blackfin snapper (Lutjanus buccanella) are known to attain a maximum fork length of 75 cm [Li = 75 cm], a size that places them among the larger members of the snapper guild inhabiting Caribbean shelf-edge reefs. This ultimate length is achieved through a protracted growth trajectory that spans several years under the warm, stable thermal conditions typical of their depth range. In contrast, the onset of reproductive capacity occurs much earlier, with individuals first reaching sexual maturity at a fork length of 28.7 cm [Lp = 28.7 cm]. This marked disparity between the length at puberty and the maximum recorded size suggests a life-history strategy in which substantial somatic investment continues well beyond the initiation of gonadal activity, a pattern observed in several iteroparous lutjanids. The corresponding body mass at this pubertal milestone has been estimated from length-weight regressions at approximately 316 grams [Wwp = approximately 316 grams], a relatively modest weight compared to the species' ultimate potential. This early maturation relative to ultimate size may confer a demographic advantage, allowing individuals to contribute to the breeding population before encountering the elevated natural mortality rates typical of larger, more exposed size classes.

Reproductive output in Lutjanus buccanella has been characterized through comparative fecundity estimates derived from closely related congeners. At a temperature of 22.3 °C [T = 22.3 °C], a female of approximately 48.5 cm total length produces an estimated 749,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 749,000 eggs per spawning event], and with approximately 6.4 spawning events per year [F_R_i = approximately 6.4 spawning events per year], this yields an annual reproductive output of approximately 4.8 million eggs, a figure that underscores the high fecundity typical of tropical lutjanids. This annual egg production reflects the combined effect of multiple spawning events within a single reproductive season, as females of this genus are known to be batch spawners that release oocytes in several distinct clutches over the course of several months. The reproductive rate is heavily influenced by ambient temperature, with the 22.3 °C [T = 22.3 °C] isotherm representing conditions commonly encountered by this species on the deeper portions of the continental slope. Such high fecundity is ecologically meaningful, offsetting the substantial losses experienced during the extended pelagic larval phase and ensuring that a sufficient number of recruits reach suitable benthic settlement habitats each year.

Neonatal body mass in Blackfin snapper is exceptionally low, with newly hatched larvae weighing approximately 0.00032 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00032 grams] upon emergence from the chorion. This minute mass, which corresponds to a larval size of roughly 2 to 3 millimeters, is consistent with the small egg diameter of 0.85 millimeters documented in the congener Lutjanus stellatus and reflects a strategy of producing large numbers of small, pelagic offspring rather than fewer, larger, demersal young. The tiny yolk-sac larva is entirely dependent on its endogenous reserves during the first few days following eclosion, before the mouth opens and the exotrophic transition begins. During this lecithotrophic stage, the larval body mass may actually decline slightly as the yolk is metabolized before exogenous feeding commences. This initial body mass serves as the starting point for a rapid growth trajectory that, under favorable thermal conditions, can see individuals increase their weight by several orders of magnitude within the first year of life as they progress through the planktonic larval and early juvenile stages.

The ultimate wet weight of Blackfin snapper has been estimated at 5,481 grams [Wwi = 5,481 grams] based on the asymptotic length of 75 cm and established length-weight relationships for the genus. This maximum body mass, equivalent to roughly 5.5 kilograms, is achieved by the oldest and largest individuals in the population, typically those that have successfully avoided predation and fishing mortality for an extended period. Such a substantial adult body mass is associated with a diet that shifts from small crustaceans and zooplankton in the juvenile stage to a piscivorous diet dominated by reef fishes and large benthic invertebrates in adulthood. The energetic demands of maintaining this large body mass are considerable, particularly in the warm waters of the Caribbean where basal metabolic rates are elevated. In comparative terms, the 5,481 gram [Wwi = 5,481 gram] ultimate weight of Lutjanus buccanella is intermediate among Caribbean snappers, being smaller than the Cubera snapper but substantially larger than the Mahogany snapper, a pattern that correlates with differences in maximum depth distribution and preferred prey size.

Maximum lifespan in Blackfin snapper, based on otolith-based age estimates from wild populations, has been reported as approximately 4,015 days [am = approximately 4,015 days] under the thermal conditions typical of their habitat at 22.3 °C [T = 22.3 °C]. This longevity, equivalent to roughly 11 years, is consistent with the moderate lifespan expected for a teleost of this body size and trophic position within the Lutjanidae family. The growth trajectory of this species decelerates markedly after puberty, and the rate at which individuals approach the 5,481 gram asymptotic mass varies with local thermal regimes; cooler slope waters may extend the time required to reach ultimate size, whereas warmer inshore areas may accelerate growth but also elevate metabolic costs. The mortality schedule in this species is thought to be characterized by relatively low adult mortality once individuals reach the size refuge provided by their large body mass, although fishing pressure represents a significant anthropogenic source of mortality that may truncate the natural age distribution. Long-term mark-recapture studies would be valuable for validating these otolith-based longevity estimates and for understanding how spatial variation in temperature, specifically deviations from the 22.3 °C [T = 22.3 °C] mean, might accelerate or decelerate the aging process across the species' geographic range.
